text: Fremont was incorporated in January 1956 out of five towns: Centerville, Irvington, Mission San José, Niles and Warm Springs.
The city is named for John C. Frémont. He died in 1890, 66 years before there was a Fremont to live in.
Mission San José was founded in June 1797, the fourteenth of California's twenty-one missions.
Charlie Chaplin made five films in Niles in 1915, one of them The Tramp. He had invented the character the year before, at Keystone in Los Angeles.
Essanay shot about 350 films in Niles between 1912 and 1916: westerns, Snakeville comedies and five Chaplins.
Broncho Billy Anderson arrived in Niles in April 1912 with 52 people. He picked the town for its weather and the canyon.
The pole at the top of Mission Peak is called the Mission Peeker. There is usually a line to get a photo beside it.
The tallest point in the City of Fremont's logo is Mission Peak.
The Tesla plant in south Fremont was NUMMI from 1984 to 2010, a General Motors and Toyota joint venture.
The first vehicle came off the Fremont assembly line in 1963. GM closed the plant in 1982, and nothing was built there until NUMMI opened two years later.
The first transcontinental railroad ran west through Niles Canyon. The heritage line there runs the same route on track relaid from 1987.
The Hayward Fault runs along the foot of the hills through east Fremont and ends in Warm Springs. It creeps. You can find curbs it has bent.
The Ohlone lived here for thousands of years before the mission. Ohlone College was named for them in 1967.
Fremont has one of the largest Afghan communities in the United States, along Fremont Boulevard.
The Dumbarton Bridge of 1927 was the first vehicular bridge across San Francisco Bay. It was demolished in 1984. The one you drive opened in 1982.
Ardenwood is a working farm with draft horses, on land the city owns and the East Bay Regional Park District has run since 1985.
Fremont covers 78 square miles. Only San Jose is larger in the Bay Area.
Mission San José's adobe church was finished in 1809 and shaken down by the 1868 earthquake. The replica you can visit was rededicated in 1985.
Until 1906 took the name, the great San Francisco earthquake meant the one in 1868. Its rupture ended in what is now Warm Springs.
On the last Sunday in August an antique flea market closes several blocks of Niles Boulevard. It has run for over sixty years.
The Shinn family settled here in 1856 and started Shinn's Nurseries in 1871. The house and grounds became a public park in 1962.
Washington High served the whole township from 1891. The other four high schools were built between 1961 and 1972 — after the five towns had merged.
Warm Springs is named for actual warm springs. They fed a resort hotel until the 1868 earthquake wrecked it. Leland Stanford made the site a winery.
Lake Elizabeth is man-made. It was dug out of Stivers Lagoon marsh in 1968.
BART reached Fremont in September 1972 and stopped there for forty-four years. Warm Springs opened in March 2017.
The Dominican Sisters at Mission San José tend about 200 mission-era olive trees, the largest surviving stand in California.
Niles is named for Addison Niles, the Central Pacific's attorney, when the junction opened in 1870. He joined the state Supreme Court two years later.
Alameda Creek, State Route 84 and two rail lines all thread the same gap through Niles Canyon.
Alameda Creek drains about 700 square miles, the largest watershed emptying into San Francisco Bay. Its mouth is in Fremont.
Irvington was Washington Corners until 1884. The town picked Irving for a local judge; the railroad printed Irvington on the depot and that stuck.
Centerville dates from 1850. The railway did not reach it until 1882. The depot still stands — moved across the tracks in 1995.

text: The climb to Mission Peak from Stanford Avenue gains about 2100 feet in three miles.
The colored ponds on the bay edge are salt evaporation ponds. The greens and reds are algae that change color as the water gets saltier.
The Don Edwards refuge on Fremont's bay shore was among the first urban National Wildlife Refuges, authorized in 1972. It is still the largest.
The Victorian at Ardenwood was the Patterson family's. They farmed the land around it for three generations.
Mission San José's cemetery holds about 4800 burials. Thousands more Ohlone lie in a separate cemetery a mile down Washington Boulevard.
Niles was a rail junction from 1870. That is how the film crews got there in 1912.
The Fremont plant covers about 5.5 million square feet, one of the largest factory buildings in the world.
Fremont's council picked the Fudenna ranch in 1960, open land between the five old towns. The city building opened there in 1968.
The 1985 mission church was rebuilt with handmade adobe bricks and rawhide-lashed timbers, around a hidden steel frame.
